blocks.text: Northgate Talent Partners LLC: Firm Overview

Most of our work begins with the same telephone call. A chief executive or a board chair has a seat to fill that the company cannot fill from inside, and rather more rides on it than on any hire they have made in years. What they want to know first is whether we can reach the people who are not looking. It is a fair question, and the honest answer takes a conversation. This page is meant to lead to that conversation rather than to stand in for it.
The assignments we take

We are a retained search firm working on senior roles in the middle market: chief executives and the leaders who report to them, the functional heads underneath, and outside directors brought on for a particular kind of judgment. We do not work on contingency and we do not advertise a search. A company fills a seat of this kind once every few years. The market it needs to reach is made up almost entirely of people who are content where they are, and reaching them is slow telephone work. That is most of what a client is buying from us.
What being retained means here
The word gets used loosely in this industry, so it is worth setting down what it means in our engagement letters.

items: 1. We work the assignment exclusively and stay with it until the seat is filled. If a search turns out harder than either side expected, that is ours to solve and not an occasion to renegotiate.
2. Expenses are billed at cost and itemized. We do not bill research time, telephone, courier, or administrative support, and we do not mark up an expense.
3. If the executive we place leaves inside the first year, for a reason other than a change the client makes to the role, we run the replacement search and bill only what it costs us out of pocket.

blocks.text: One consultant, first meeting to first month in the seat

The firm is small deliberately. The consultant who takes the first meeting writes the specification, makes the approaches, and sits in the room when the finalists are argued over. Nothing is sold by one person and worked by another. Behind that consultant is a research bench that has grown steadily with the practice, and its work is the part clients tend to underestimate. Before there is a slate, somebody has to establish who holds this job today, at which companies, in which markets, and which of those people will take a call at all. A slate is only ever as good as the map it came off. The specification comes first and the client corrects it line by line, because a document nobody argued with is a document nobody agreed to.
How we speak about people who are not yet candidates

Discretion here is a habit rather than a policy. In anything that travels past the hiring executive, a person is the role they hold now and the sector they hold it in, never a name. A prospect learns which company we are calling for when there is a real conversation to be had, and not before. The discipline costs us nothing. It is the reason a senior person takes our second call as readily as the first, and it is the reason we are able to go back to someone two years later about a different seat.

blocks.text: A reference conversation with a client who has been through a search with us will tell a board more than any list of names, and we are glad to arrange one. If a search is being weighed now, the next step is a half hour on the telephone with Kelly Chavez, our Managing Director. She takes the first call on every assignment. If we are the wrong firm for it, she will say so on that call.
Jeffrey and James,

Building management is changing the lobby readers this week, and the two of you are in well before the front desk is staffed, so this lands on you harder than on the rest of us. From Wednesday the side entrance stays locked until eight and the cards we hold now will not open it. The replacements are at the desk in the lobby, and they want the old cards handed back when you collect.
The building is shut Thursday and Friday for the holiday. If either of you means to come in over the long weekend, tell me today and I will have the access added before we close tomorrow.
Sincerely
Larry Russell, Research Associate

Larry Russell joined the search practice on Monday as a Research Associate, and we are glad to have him. Take this as the file copy and as a welcome. Four of us met him separately before the offer went out, and what came back each time was a note about temperament rather than technique, which does not happen often and which, for this seat, is the right way round.

Larry has the hard end of the list. Every search reaches a stretch where the obvious people have said no, the client is getting anxious, and the work becomes ringing someone who declined in the spring to ask what has changed since. Most people are not built for that. He is patient with a slow process and comfortable going back a second time, and he would rather make the call than write around it. He reports to Sandra Fuentes, Principal. She sets what he works and in what order.

It is worth saying plainly why the firm pays for patience. From the outside, a search that ends well looks like a lucky introduction. From the inside it is a long run of conversations that went nowhere and one that did not, and nobody is owed that last one. It is earned by working the list after the interesting part is over, and by leaving the kind of impression that lets us call the same person again next year about something else entirely.
Three things for the first month:

items: 1. Discretion is the house rule and it does not bend. Outside the search file a candidate is the job they hold now, never a name.

2. A call is not a record until it is written down. Summarizing it in a handful of lines is fine, as long as the lines are in the file the same day, because the consultant reading them on a Sunday cannot ring you to ask what you meant.
3. When a prospect asks who the client is, that answer comes from the consultant carrying the search.

blocks.text: Kelly Chavez will take an hour with him in the next fortnight on how this firm describes a candidate to a client and what we will not put in writing. That hour is the one conversation here nobody skips. Before then, Sandra Fuentes hands over the specification and the target list on an open assignment Thursday morning, and he should expect to be on the telephone with it before the week is out.
New this week: Mary Parker

Mary Parker started with us this week as a Research Associate, and she is welcome. She comes from work where an answer had to be right before it was allowed to be interesting, and it shows in how she writes: short flat statements, numbered as often as not, and no more of them than the point requires.

Her seat is verification, and it is the seat that keeps a slate defensible. Before a name reaches a client, somebody has to establish what that person actually owns today, how large the team really is, what the line they carry actually covers, and where the story a resume tells goes thin. Mary does that work and keeps what she has confirmed strictly apart from what she was told. The consultants will learn quickly that when her note hedges, the hedge is the finding, and that the right response is another question rather than a rounded-up sentence. She reports to Sandra Fuentes, Principal, and will take work from every consultant in the practice, so an early skill is saying what she can finish and by when.

From outside the firm this can look like checking. It is closer to protecting the client and the candidate at the same time. A retained search is sold on the promise that the four or five people in front of a board have been assessed rather than merely admired, and a slate that has not been verified will eventually put a client in a room with a person whose job is smaller than the paper suggested. That conversation is expensive for everybody in it, and it is avoidable. Mary is one of the reasons we can avoid it.
Three standing rules for the first month:

items: 1. Confirmed and reported are two columns and they never merge. If a figure came from the candidate, the note says so in the same line.
2. Nothing about a prospect travels outside the search file. Current role and sector will carry almost any sentence you need to write.
3. If verification turns up something that changes the slate, it goes to the consultant carrying the search that day, not at the end of the week.

blocks.text: Kelly Chavez will sit down with her inside the first fortnight on our written standards for describing a candidate, which are stricter than most people arrive with, and the short version is that we write as though the note will be read aloud to the client and the candidate both. Her first piece of work is the verification pass on an open file. Sandra Fuentes will hand it over Monday morning and wants her first questions back before that week closes.
Hello Nicole,

I am copying the office so that this only goes round once: the server that holds the research files and the shared calendar comes down for maintenance early on Saturday, and while it is meant to be back the same afternoon, nobody should build a weekend around that.

Three things follow from it. Anything you expect to need over the weekend should be on your own machine before you leave Friday, the telephones and the answering service are untouched, and mail sent into the office while the work is running will arrive late rather than not at all. Nicole Donovan is keeping the list of what has to stay reachable, so send her whatever belongs on it by Thursday and she will close the list before the technician starts.
Regards
Northgate Talent Partners LLC: Firm Overview

Northgate Talent Partners is a retained executive search firm. We fill senior operating roles and board seats for companies in the middle market, and one consultant carries an assignment from the first meeting to the new executive's first month in the seat. What follows is a short account of how the practice works, written for a board or a chief executive with a search in prospect.
Can you reach the people who are not looking?

That is the whole job. The people worth having are employed, well regarded, and reading nothing that resembles an advertisement. Reaching them is telephone work against a map of the market, and the map gets built before a single name goes in front of a client. Larry Russell works the hard end of those lists here, the roles where the obvious people have already said no, and he is patient about going back to someone who declined the first time. Much of what he learns never reaches a document. It shows up in who we call next.
Will the slate stand up?

A short slate is easy to assemble and hard to defend, and ours is defensible because somebody checks it. Mary Parker establishes what a prospect actually owns today and where the story a resume tells goes thin, keeping what she has confirmed apart from what she was told. When her note hedges, the hedge is the finding, and it reaches the client in those words. A board should hear that from us and not discover it in a reference call.
Who actually does the work?

The consultant a client meets first. The firm is small on purpose, and nothing here is sold by one person and worked by another. The research bench sits behind that consultant and has grown as the practice has, but the specification, the approaches, and the assessment stay with one named person from beginning to end. A client always knows whose telephone to pick up, and that person always knows the search well enough to answer without going away to check.
What we put in writing
Three commitments, and they appear in every engagement letter we sign.

items: 1. A written position specification, agreed line by line before we approach anybody. Every candidate is measured against it, and so are we.
2. Written reporting on a fixed rhythm. The report goes out in the weeks when the news is thin as well as in the weeks when it is good, because a quiet month is still a month the client has paid for.
3. Candidates described by current role and sector, never by name, in anything that circulates. A name reaches a client when one of us can say precisely why it belongs there.

blocks.text: Two further terms are worth stating on a page like this, because they are the ones clients ask about last and care about most. We work on retainer rather than on contingency, so a client is buying a search and not a placement, and expenses are billed at cost without a markup. And for as long as an engagement is open, and for a year after it closes, we will not approach anyone employed by that client on behalf of another. A firm that recruits out of the company it just recruited into is not one a board should keep on retainer.

One change since we last revised this page is worth noting. More of our first meetings now happen over video than across a table, and for an opening conversation it has worked better than we expected, particularly with people who cannot easily be seen leaving their own building in the middle of a working day. We still sit down in person with a finalist before that finalist goes in front of a board.
